title: Euler buckling: the critical load that makes a slender column bow
examples: How do end conditions affect buckling?
Why do long columns buckle instead of crushing?

explain.say: Press the ends of a plastic ruler together. Nothing happens, nothing happens, and then it suddenly bows out sideways. It has not crushed; it has buckled. In 1744 Leonhard Euler worked out the exact load where this happens. Look at the two equal pushes squeezing the ruler.

draw.text: Euler buckling: the critical load that makes a slender column bow
Buckling: a sudden sideways bowing under compression

explain.say: Euler's critical load is pi squared E I over L squared, for a column pinned at both ends. Take a solid steel rod 20 millimetres across and 1 metre long. I is about 7850 millimetres to the fourth, so P critical is about 15.5 kilonewtons. See the curve on the graph? What happens when the rod gets longer?

curves.label: Crushing 78.5 kN
curves.ask: Why do long columns buckle instead of crushing?

explain.say: It falls fast, with one over L squared: double the length, a quarter of the load. The ends matter too. Replace L by the effective length, K times L. A flagpole fixed at the bottom and free at the top has K equals 2: only 3.9 kilonewtons. Fixed at both ends, K is 0.5: 62 kilonewtons. See the bars? Which end condition is strongest?

Fixed at both ends, sixteen times the flagpole! But Euler is not the whole story. A short rod crushes first, when the stress reaches yield: 250 megapascals times 314 square millimetres, about 78.5 kilonewtons. See the flat line? Long columns buckle below it; very short ones crush. Where does our 1 metre rod fall?

curves.label: Crushing 78.5 kN
curves.ask: Why do long columns buckle instead of crushing?

explain.say: Well below the crushing line, so it buckles. Great work! Real link: scaffolding tubes, bicycle frames and building columns are all checked for buckling, and bracing halfway shortens the effective length. Exam tip: buckling happens about the axis with the smaller I, so check the weak direction. Challenge: what is P critical for a 2 metre pinned rod?

faq.a: Buckling is a sudden sideways bending of a slender member under compression. It can happen at a stress well below the material's yield strength.
asks: what happens when a column buckles

faq.a: P critical equals pi squared E I over the effective length squared. It gives the axial load at which a slender, straight, elastic column buckles.

faq.q: How do end conditions affect buckling?
faq.a: They change the effective length, K times L. Fixed-free has K of 2, pinned-pinned 1, and fixed-fixed 0.5, so fixed ends allow a much bigger load.
It is the effective length divided by the radius of gyration of the section. High slenderness means a column will buckle rather than crush.

faq.q: Why do long columns buckle instead of crushing?
faq.a: The buckling load falls with one over length squared, while the crushing load does not depend on length. For a long column the buckling load is reached first.

facts: The Euler critical load of a pinned-pinned column is pi squared E I over L squared.
A column fixed at both ends has an effective length of half its actual length.

quiz.say: A pinned column has a critical load of 40 kilonewtons. What is the critical load if its length doubles?
quiz.show: A pinned column buckles at 40 kN. Length doubled: new P_cr?
quiz.why: P_cr goes as 1 / L², so doubling L divides it by 4: 40 / 4 = 10 kN.

wrong.1: Length is squared in the formula, so it falls by four, not two.
wrong.2: A longer column is weaker, not stronger.

quiz.say: A column is fixed at the base and free at the top. What is its effective length factor K?
quiz.show: Column fixed at the base, free at the top. Effective length factor K?
quiz.why: A fixed-free column bends like half of a pinned column twice as long, so K equals 2.

wrong.1: K equals 1 is for pinned at both ends.
wrong.2: K equals 0.5 is for fixed at both ends.
